pages.text: Oceans cover seventy percent of the Earth and store vast amounts of energy. This stored energy is known as ocean heat content. It serves as an important indicator of global warming and helps scientists understand our changing climate and environmental stability over time.
pages.caption: The ocean heat content (OHC) has been increasing for decades as the ocean has been absorbing most of the excess heat resulting from greenhouse gas emissions from human activities. The graph shows OHC calculated to a water depth of 700 and 2000 meters.

pages.text: Between 1971 and 2018, oceans took in over ninety percent of the extra energy from global warming. Human greenhouse gas emissions are the main reason for this change.

pages.text: Scientists measure ocean temperatures at many different locations and depths. Since the year 2000, an expanding network of nearly four thousand robotic Argo floats has helped measure temperature anomalies and changes in ocean heat all around the world.

pages.text: Changes in ocean temperature greatly affect ecosystems in oceans and on land. Warming water affects marine life and causes variations in sea level and sea ice. It also changes the intensity of the water cycle and the migration of marine species.
pages.caption: Earth heat inventory (energy accumulation) in ZJ for the components of the Earth's climate system relative to 1960 and from 1960 to 2018. The upper ocean (0–300 m, light blue line, and 0–700 m, light blue shading) accounts for the largest amount of heat gain.

pages.text: Between 1971 and 2018, a steady upward trend in ocean heat content accounted for over ninety percent of Earth's excess energy from global warming. Increased ocean heat in response to anthropogenic carbon dioxide emissions is essentially irreversible on human time scales.

Ocean heat content measures the energy absorbed and stored by the world's oceans. Because oceans cover seventy percent of the Earth and have a high heat capacity, they play a critical role in climate stability.

C1-C2.headline: The Dynamics of Ocean Heat Uptake

pages.text: Ocean heat content quantifies the thermodynamic potential energy stored within seawater basins. Because oceans possess a high heat capacity and cover seventy percent of the planetary surface, they absorb the vast majority of excess anthropogenic heat.
pages.caption: The ocean heat content (OHC) has been increasing for decades as the ocean has been absorbing most of the excess heat resulting from greenhouse gas emissions from human activities. The graph shows OHC calculated to a water depth of 700 and 2000 meters.

evidence.articleCaption: The ocean heat content (OHC) has been increasing for decades as the ocean has been absorbing most of the excess heat resulting from greenhouse gas emissions from human activities. The graph shows OHC calculated to a water depth of 700 and 2000 meters.

pages.text: Observational data reveals a robust multi-decadal upward trajectory, with ocean heat uptake accounting for over ninety percent of Earth's net energy imbalance since 1971. This persistent warming is fundamentally driven by rising atmospheric greenhouse gases.
pages.caption: Chart of different thermoclines (depth versus ocean temperature) based on seasons and latitude

evidence.articleCaption: Chart of different thermoclines (depth versus ocean temperature) based on seasons and latitude

pages.text: Historical assessments relied on research vessels and stations, whereas contemporary monitoring utilizes approximately four thousand robotic profiling floats deployed through the international Argo program to measure subsurface temperature anomalies and track regional variations in heat uptake.
pages.caption: The global distribution of active floats in the Argo array

evidence.articleCaption: The global distribution of active floats in the Argo array

pages.text: Regional variations in heat uptake are pronounced. The extratropical Southern Ocean has absorbed a disproportionate share of thermal energy, contributing to regional sea ice reduction and influencing global overturning circulation.
pages.caption: Earth heat inventory (energy accumulation) in ZJ for the components of the Earth's climate system relative to 1960 and from 1960 to 2018. The upper ocean (0–300 m, light blue line, and 0–700 m, light blue shading) accounts for the largest amount of heat gain.

evidence.articleCaption: Earth heat inventory (energy accumulation) in ZJ for the components of the Earth's climate system relative to 1960 and from 1960 to 2018. The upper ocean (0–300 m, light blue line, and 0–700 m, light blue shading) accounts for the largest amount of heat gain.

pages.text: The resulting thermal expansion drives ongoing sea level rise and triggers ecological disruptions such as coral bleaching. Due to the immense thermal inertia of the oceans, these increases remain virtually irreversible on human time scales.
